summary: Inflammatory GI diseases run from reflux, esophagitis, gastritis, and ulcers in the upper tract to appendicitis, diverticular disease, and inflammatory bowel disease lower down. Exams test what injures the mucosa, where the lesion sits, and which complication follows.

points: GERD comes from transient LES relaxations, low resting LES tone, and hiatal hernia.
Risks: obesity and pregnancy (raised abdominal pressure; progesterone relaxes the LES), smoking, alcohol, fatty meals.
Symptoms: heartburn and regurgitation; aspiration and vagal reflexes add chronic cough, hoarseness, and wheeze.
Reflux esophagitis biopsy: basal cell hyperplasia, elongated lamina propria papillae, a few eosinophils.
Complications: peptic stricture with dysphagia, ulcer, bleeding, and Barrett esophagus.
Barrett: distal squamous epithelium replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells; then low-grade dysplasia, high-grade dysplasia, adenocarcinoma.
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopic young men, dysphagia and food impaction, 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, rings and linear furrows.
Pill esophagitis: doxycycline, NSAIDs, potassium chloride, bisphosphonates; a pill taken with little water while lying down sits and burns a focal ulcer.
Mallory-Weiss: longitudinal mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful retching (alcohol use, bulimia); hematemesis.
Boerhaave: full-thickness rupture, usually the distal left wall; severe chest pain, pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysema, mediastinitis.
NSAIDs block COX, so less prostaglandin: less mucus and bicarbonate, less mucosal blood flow, more acid.
Alcohol, uremia, and shock also cause acute erosive gastritis.
Curling ulcer: severe burns cause hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia. Cushing ulcer: brain injury raises vagal output, so acid rises.
H. pylori gastritis starts in the antrum; urease makes ammonia; leads to intestinal metaplasia, adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma, and duodenal ulcer.
Autoimmune gastritis hits the body and fundus; T cells and antibodies destroy parietal cells, giving achlorhydria, high gastrin, and pernicious anemia.
H. pylori and NSAIDs cause most ulcers; Zollinger-Ellison gives multiple, refractory, or distal ulcers.
H. pylori in the antrum lowers somatostatin, so gastrin and acid rise and the duodenum takes the hit.
Posterior duodenal ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery; lesser curvature gastric ulcers erode the left gastric artery.
Anterior duodenal ulcers perforate: sudden severe pain, rigid abdomen, free air under the diaphragm on an upright film.
Appendicitis: a fecalith (adults) or lymphoid hyperplasia (children) blocks the lumen; mucus builds, pressure squeezes veins then arteries, and bacteria invade the ischemic wall.
Early pain is visceral (T10 afferents), vague, and periumbilical; it moves to McBurney point once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed.
Untreated appendicitis leads to gangrene, perforation, abscess, and peritonitis.
Diverticula: a low-fiber diet makes small stools and high segmental pressure; mucosa and submucosa herniate where vasa recta pierce the muscle, mostly in the sigmoid.
Diverticulosis bleeds painlessly when a stretched vas rectum ruptures; diverticulitis gives LLQ pain, fever, leukocytosis, and can form an abscess, perforate, or make a colovesical fistula.
Crohn: anywhere mouth to anus, usually terminal ileum; skip lesions, transmural, noncaseating granulomas, cobblestone mucosa.
Ulcerative colitis: rectum first, extends proximally, continuous; mucosa and submucosa only; crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps.
Crohn complications: fistulas, strictures, B12 and bile acid malabsorption, gallstones, calcium oxalate kidney stones.
UC complications: toxic megacolon, primary sclerosing cholangitis. Both: colorectal cancer, erythema nodosum, uveitis, arthritis.
Microscopic colitis: older women, chronic watery diarrhea, normal-looking colonoscopy; only a biopsy shows it.
Collagenous colitis has a thick subepithelial collagen band; lymphocytic colitis has excess intraepithelial lymphocytes. NSAIDs, PPIs, and SSRIs are linked.
Radiation enteritis: acute crypt injury; later, obliterative endarteritis causes fibrosis, stricture, and bleeding.
Anal fissure: posterior midline tear, tearing pain with stools, bright red blood on the paper; an off-midline fissure suggests Crohn disease.

Anorectal abscess starts in an anal gland and can track to skin as a fistula (classic in Crohn). Proctitis: UC, radiation, sexually transmitted infection. Rectal prolapse: concentric rings, older women who strain, children with cystic fibrosis.

tricks.label: ULCCCERS (ulcerative colitis)
tricks.text: Ulcers, Large intestine, Continuous, Colorectal carcinoma, Crypt abscesses, Extends proximally, Red diarrhea, Sclerosing cholangitis.

tricks.label: Meals sort the ulcer
tricks.text: Gastric ulcer pain gets worse when food arrives, so patients eat less and lose weight. Duodenal ulcer pain eases with food because the meal buffers acid, then it returns hours later.

tricks.label: Appendicitis pain moves
tricks.text: Visceral fibers from the appendix enter at T10, so early pain is vague and around the navel. When the inflamed tip touches the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic nerves, pain localizes to McBurney point.

tricks.label: Tear versus rupture
tricks.text: Mallory-Weiss tears the mucosa only, so blood comes up. Boerhaave goes all the way through, so air escapes into the mediastinum and under the skin.

highYield: Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells and is the precursor of esophageal adenocarcinoma.
Autoimmune gastritis in the body and fundus causes achlorhydria, high gastrin, and pernicious anemia.
Posterior duodenal ulcers bleed from the gastroduodenal artery; anterior ones perforate.
Curling ulcer follows burns from ischemia; Cushing ulcer follows brain injury from vagal acid drive.
Colonic diverticula are false diverticula at sites where vasa recta pierce the muscle.
Noncaseating granulomas and transmural inflammation point to Crohn disease.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis and toxic megacolon go with ulcerative colitis.
Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhea with normal-looking mucosa on colonoscopy.
pitfalls: Calcium oxalate stones in Crohn disease come from fat binding calcium in the gut, which leaves oxalate free to be absorbed; they do not mean a calcium excess.
Eosinophils appear in both reflux and eosinophilic esophagitis; the eosinophilic type has 15 or more per high-power field and involves the upper esophagus too.
Diverticulosis bleeding is painless; pain with fever means diverticulitis.
Autoimmune gastritis has high gastrin because acid is absent; a high gastrin with high acid points to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
A fissure off the posterior midline is atypical and should raise concern for Crohn disease or another cause.

summary: Congenital GI disease comes from steps in gut, face, and abdominal wall development that fail or go wrong. Exams test the defect behind each condition, the age it shows up, and the clue that names it, such as bilious versus nonbilious vomiting.

points: Faulty division of the foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum.
Most common type: blind upper esophageal pouch with a fistula from the trachea to the distal esophagus.
Fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid, so polyhydramnios.
Newborn drools, chokes, coughs, and turns cyanotic with the first feeds; a nasogastric tube coils in the pouch.
Air in the stomach on x-ray means a distal fistula; a gasless abdomen means atresia without a distal fistula.
Look for VACTERL defects (vertebral, anal, cardiac, TE fistula, renal, limb).
Esophageal web: thin mucosal fold in the upper esophagus; dysphagia to solids.
Plummer-Vinson: web plus iron deficiency anemia and dysphagia; raises squamous cell carcinoma risk.
Schatzki ring: lower esophageal ring at the squamocolumnar junction; intermittent dysphagia with solid food such as meat.
Meckel: persistent vitelline duct forming a true diverticulum (all wall layers) on the antimesenteric ileum.
Ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid and ulcerates nearby ileum, giving painless rectal bleeding in a young child.
Meckel can also act as a lead point for intussusception, twist into volvulus, or inflame and mimic appendicitis.
Hypertrophy of pyloric smooth muscle narrows the outlet.
Starts at 2 to 6 weeks: nonbilious projectile vomiting after feeds, hungry infant, olive-shaped epigastric mass.
Loss of gastric HCl gives hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; volume loss drives aldosterone, so the kidney wastes potassium (hypokalemia).
Risks: first-born males, macrolide exposure (erythromycin, azithromycin) in early infancy.
Progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts.
First weeks of life: persistent conjugated jaundice, acholic (pale) stools, dark urine, hepatomegaly.
Without surgery it progresses to biliary cirrhosis; it is the most common reason for liver transplant in children.
Gastroschisis: full-thickness defect, usually right of the umbilicus; bowel lies free with no covering sac.
Omphalocele: midline; midgut fails to return after physiologic herniation; covered by peritoneum and amnion; linked to trisomy 13 and 18 and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
Malrotation: incomplete 270 degree counterclockwise rotation leaves the cecum in the upper right abdomen.
Ladd bands run from the misplaced cecum across the duodenum and obstruct it; the narrow mesentery can twist (midgut volvulus), causing bilious vomiting and bowel ischemia.
Cleft lip: maxillary prominence fails to fuse with the medial nasal prominence.
Cleft palate: palatine shelves fail to fuse with each other or with the primary palate.
Infant cannot seal and suck well: poor feeding, nasal regurgitation, aspiration; later ear infections and speech problems.

tricks.label: Rule of 2s (Meckel diverticulum)
tricks.text: About 2 percent of people, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric and pancreatic), often shows up by age 2, about 2 times more common in males.

tricks.label: VACTERL
tricks.text: Vertebral defects, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, Tracheoesophageal fistula, Renal defects, Limb defects (often radial).

tricks.label: Sac or no sac
tricks.text: Omphalocele has a sac and sits in the midline, and it often comes with other defects. Gastroschisis has no sac and sits beside the cord, and the bowel is usually the only problem.

tricks.label: Green means emergency
tricks.text: Bile in a newborn's vomit means the block is past the ampulla. Treat it as malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.

highYield: The most common esophageal atresia has a distal tracheoesophageal fistula, so the stomach contains air.
Polyhydramnios points to a fetus that cannot swallow, as in esophageal atresia.
Pyloric stenosis gives hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum; painless bleeding comes from acid made by ectopic gastric mucosa.
Plummer-Vinson syndrome: esophageal web, iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, and squamous cell carcinoma risk.
Biliary atresia causes persistent conjugated jaundice with pale stools in the first weeks of life.
Omphalocele is covered by peritoneum and amnion and goes with trisomies and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
pitfalls: Physiologic newborn jaundice is unconjugated and fades in the first two weeks; jaundice that stays and is conjugated needs a biliary atresia workup.
Pyloric stenosis vomit has no bile because the block is above the ampulla; bilious vomit points to malrotation or atresia below it.
Esophageal web sits high (upper esophagus); Schatzki ring sits low at the squamocolumnar junction.
Cleft lip and cleft palate come from different fusion failures and can occur alone or together.

summary: The abdominal cavity can fill with fluid (ascites), become infected (peritonitis), or scar after injury (adhesions). Exams test why fluid builds in cirrhosis, how to read the ascitic fluid, and how to tell spontaneous from secondary peritonitis.

points: Portal hypertension raises hydrostatic pressure in the hepatic sinusoids and splanchnic capillaries.
Low albumin from liver failure lowers plasma oncotic pressure.
Splanchnic vasodilation (nitric oxide) makes arteries feel underfilled, so renin, angiotensin, aldosterone, ADH, and sympathetic tone rise.
The kidney retains sodium and water, and the extra fluid leaks into the peritoneum.
Exam: bulging flanks, shifting dullness, fluid wave.
SAAG = serum albumin minus ascitic fluid albumin.
SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more means portal hypertension: cirrhosis, heart failure, Budd-Chiari syndrome.
SAAG under 1.1 g/dL means another cause: peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculous peritonitis, nephrotic syndrome, pancreatitis.
Ascitic neutrophils of 250/mm3 or more mean infection.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP): infected cirrhotic ascites with no surgical source; gut bacteria cross the wall.
SBP organisms: usually one gram-negative enteric rod, E. coli or Klebsiella.
Low ascitic protein (under about 1.5 g/dL) means little complement and opsonin, which raises SBP risk.
SBP can be subtle: fever, mild diffuse tenderness, new confusion, or worsening kidney function.
Secondary peritonitis: perforated ulcer, appendix, or diverticulum; polymicrobial with anaerobes such as Bacteroides fragilis.
Secondary peritonitis gives a rigid, board-like abdomen, rebound, guarding, and free air on imaging.
Surgery, infection, or blood injures the mesothelium, and a fibrin exudate forms.
Injured mesothelium makes less plasminogen activator, so fibrin persists and fibroblasts turn it into fibrous bands.
Main complication: small bowel obstruction with colicky pain, vomiting, distension, and no flatus.
Adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults; a closed loop can strangulate.

tricks.label: High gradient, high pressure
tricks.text: A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more means fluid was pushed out by high portal pressure. A low SAAG means something on the peritoneum itself, such as tumor or infection, is leaking protein-rich fluid.

tricks.label: One bug or many
tricks.text: One gram-negative rod in ascitic fluid fits spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Many organisms, including anaerobes, mean a hole in the bowel.

highYield: A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more means portal hypertension.
Ascitic neutrophils of 250/mm3 or more diagnose spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
E. coli and Klebsiella are the usual causes of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Splanchnic vasodilation and RAAS activation make the kidney retain sodium in cirrhosis.
Secondary peritonitis is polymicrobial and causes a rigid abdomen.
Adhesions are the leading cause of small bowel obstruction in adults.
pitfalls: Cirrhosis has total body sodium overload even when serum sodium is low; the low serum sodium reflects ADH-driven water retention.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis may show no rigidity; new confusion or kidney injury in a cirrhotic patient is enough to tap the ascites.
Heart failure ascites also has a high SAAG; a high ascitic protein helps separate it from cirrhosis.

summary: GI vascular disease covers dilated veins (varices, hemorrhoids), dilated mucosal vessels (angiodysplasia), and lost blood supply (mesenteric ischemia, necrotizing enterocolitis). Exams test the vessel involved, where it bleeds or infarcts, and the setting that predicts it.

points: Portal hypertension opens portosystemic shunts.
Left gastric vein (portal) connects to esophageal veins that drain to the azygos system (systemic).
Distal esophageal submucosal veins dilate and can rupture.
Rupture causes painless, massive hematemesis, a major cause of death in cirrhosis.
Low platelets from splenic sequestration and low clotting factors make bleeding worse.
Dilated, sliding anal vascular cushions.
Internal: above the pectinate line, visceral nerves, so painless bright red bleeding and prolapse.
External: below the pectinate line, somatic nerves (inferior rectal), so painful when thrombosed.
Risks: straining, constipation, low-fiber diet, pregnancy, prolonged sitting.
Acute: embolus from atrial fibrillation or mural thrombus lodges in the superior mesenteric artery (SMA).
Pain out of proportion to the exam, then raised lactate, metabolic acidosis, bloody stool, and peritonitis.
Other acute causes: SMA thrombosis on atherosclerosis, low-flow states (shock), mesenteric vein thrombosis.
Mucosa dies first; full-thickness infarction leads to perforation and sepsis.
Chronic: atherosclerosis of the mesenteric arteries; pain soon after meals, food fear, weight loss.
Ischemic colitis: low flow to watershed zones (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction); older adult with crampy pain then bloody diarrhea.
Dilated, tortuous submucosal vessels, mostly in the cecum and right colon of adults over 60.
High wall tension in the wide cecum partly blocks submucosal veins during contraction, so they dilate over years.
Painless, intermittent lower GI bleeding and iron deficiency anemia.
Heyde syndrome: aortic stenosis shear breaks up large von Willebrand factor multimers, so angiodysplasia bleeds more.
Also linked to end-stage kidney disease.
Premature infant, usually after enteral (often formula) feeds start; breast milk lowers risk.
Immature mucosa, poor blood flow, and bacterial invasion cause mucosal necrosis, often terminal ileum and colon.
Feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, bloody stools.
X-ray: pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in the bowel wall), portal venous gas, free air if perforated.

tricks.label: Pectinate line sorts pain
tricks.text: Above the line has visceral nerves, so internal hemorrhoids do not hurt. Below the line has somatic nerves, so external hemorrhoids hurt when they clot.

tricks.label: Watershed zones of the colon
tricks.text: The splenic flexure sits between SMA and IMA territory, and the rectosigmoid sits between IMA and internal iliac territory. Low flow injures these edges first.

tricks.label: Heyde: murmur plus bleeding
tricks.text: An older patient with an aortic stenosis murmur and iron deficiency from painless GI bleeding has Heyde syndrome until proven otherwise.

highYield: Esophageal varices form where the left gastric vein meets esophageal veins draining to the azygos system.
Variceal bleeding is painless massive hematemesis in a patient with cirrhosis.
Internal hemorrhoids bleed painlessly; thrombosed external hemorrhoids hurt.
Acute mesenteric ischemia gives pain out of proportion to the exam; atrial fibrillation is the classic embolic source.
Chronic mesenteric ischemia gives postprandial pain and weight loss from food fear.
Angiodysplasia is in the cecum and right colon and links to aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome).
Pneumatosis intestinalis in a premature infant means necrotizing enterocolitis.
pitfalls: Hemorrhoids are not caused by portal hypertension; portal hypertension makes anorectal varices, a different lesion.
Mallory-Weiss tears also cause hematemesis after retching, but the bleed is usually smaller and the patient may have no liver disease.
Early acute mesenteric ischemia has a soft abdomen; waiting for peritoneal signs means the bowel is already dying.
Ischemic colitis affects the colon watershed areas and usually recovers; acute mesenteric ischemia involves the SMA and small bowel and is more lethal.

summary: GI neoplasms run from the mouth and salivary glands to the anus, plus the liver, pancreas, and bile ducts. Exams test each tumor's risk factors and precursor lesion, where it grows, its marker, and the sign that shows it has spread.

points: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: upper and middle third; alcohol, tobacco, achalasia, caustic injury, Plummer-Vinson.
Esophageal adenocarcinoma: distal third; GERD, Barrett esophagus, obesity.
Both cause progressive dysphagia, solids then liquids, with weight loss.
Intestinal-type gastric cancer: H. pylori, nitrosamines in smoked foods, atrophic gastritis; forms glands.
Diffuse-type gastric cancer: signet ring cells, thick rigid stomach (linitis plastica), loss of E-cadherin (CDH1).
Spread: Virchow node (left supraclavicular), Sister Mary Joseph nodule (umbilicus), Krukenberg tumor (ovaries).
MALT lymphoma: extranodal marginal zone B cell lymphoma driven by H. pylori; early lesions can regress when H. pylori is cleared.
GIST: KIT (CD117) mutant tumor of the interstitial cells of Cajal, most often in the stomach.
Zollinger-Ellison: gastrinoma in the duodenum or pancreas; about a quarter occur in MEN1.
Gastrin drives acid: multiple, refractory, or distal (jejunal) ulcers.
Acid inactivates pancreatic lipase and precipitates bile acids, so diarrhea and steatorrhea.
Secretin normally lowers gastrin; in gastrinoma it paradoxically raises it.
Small bowel carcinoid makes serotonin; the liver breaks it down, so carcinoid syndrome appears mainly after liver metastasis.
Carcinoid syndrome: flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, right-sided valve fibrosis; raised urinary 5-HIAA.
Hepatocellular carcinoma risks: chronic HBV (even without cirrhosis), HCV, alcohol, hemochromatosis, aflatoxin B1 (TP53 mutation).
Findings: raised alpha-fetoprotein, enlarging liver, weight loss; spreads through blood vessels (portal and hepatic veins).
Metastases are the most common malignancy in the liver and on the peritoneum.
Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor.
Hepatocellular adenoma: oral contraceptive or anabolic steroid use; can rupture and bleed.
Oral leukoplakia: white plaque that does not scrape off; may hide dysplasia, so biopsy.
Oral squamous cell carcinoma: tobacco and alcohol. Oropharyngeal carcinoma: HPV-16.
Pleomorphic adenoma: most common salivary tumor, usually parotid, epithelial plus stromal tissue; recurs if incompletely removed.
Warthin tumor: parotid, smokers, cysts with lymphoid stroma. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma: most common salivary malignancy.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: KRAS mutation; risks smoking and chronic pancreatitis.
Head tumors: painless jaundice with a palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign); also migratory thrombophlebitis, weight loss, raised CA 19-9.
Cholangiocarcinoma: primary sclerosing cholangitis, liver flukes such as Clonorchis sinensis; painless obstructive jaundice.
Gallbladder adenocarcinoma: gallstones. Anal squamous cell carcinoma: below the pectinate line, HPV-related.
Right-sided cancer: bulky mass, occult bleeding, iron deficiency anemia.
Left-sided cancer: napkin-ring narrowing, change in bowel habit, obstruction, visible blood.
Risks: age, IBD, familial adenomatous polyposis (APC), Lynch syndrome (mismatch repair genes).
CEA tracks recurrence after surgery; it is not a screening test.
Adenoma malignancy risk rises with size and villous component.

tricks.label: Squamous up top, adeno at the bottom
tricks.text: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma sits high where the lining is squamous and the irritants pass. Adenocarcinoma sits low where acid makes Barrett glandular lining.

tricks.label: Why carcinoid needs the liver
tricks.text: Gut serotonin goes to the liver through the portal vein and is broken down there. Once tumor is in the liver, serotonin reaches the systemic circulation, and the lungs clear it before the left heart, so the right-sided valves scar.

tricks.label: Right bleeds, left blocks
tricks.text: The right colon is wide with liquid stool, so tumors grow large and bleed slowly. The left colon is narrow with formed stool, so tumors obstruct.

highYield: Barrett esophagus leads to distal esophageal adenocarcinoma; alcohol and tobacco lead to upper and middle squamous cell carcinoma.
Signet ring cells and linitis plastica mean diffuse gastric cancer with CDH1 loss.
Gastric MALT lymphoma is driven by H. pylori; GIST carries a KIT (CD117) mutation.
Gastrinoma raises gastrin after secretin and links to MEN1.
Carcinoid syndrome needs liver metastasis and raises urinary 5-HIAA.
Aflatoxin B1 causes TP53 mutation and hepatocellular carcinoma; HBV can cause it without cirrhosis.
Courvoisier sign: painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder points to a tumor blocking the distal bile duct, classically a pancreatic head cancer.
Villous adenomas carry the highest malignant risk of colon adenomas.
pitfalls: Metastases outnumber primary tumors in the liver; a liver mass in a patient with colon cancer is a metastasis until proven otherwise.
Leukoplakia and candidiasis both look white; candidiasis scrapes off and leukoplakia does not.
CEA helps follow colon cancer after surgery and should not be used to screen.
Hyperplastic polyps are usually harmless; sessile serrated lesions look similar but are premalignant.
Warthin tumor is benign and occurs in smokers; mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common salivary malignancy.

Pancreatic head: adenocarcinoma with KRAS; Courvoisier sign, CA 19-9
Colon: adenocarcinoma from adenomas; CEA for recurrence
Anus below the pectinate line: squamous cell carcinoma with HPV

summary: Infectious GI diseases include diarrheal illness, infections of the mouth and esophagus, viral hepatitis, and liver abscess. Exams link each organism to its setting, the way it causes damage, and the complication it is known for.

points: Antibiotics (clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins) wipe out normal colonic flora.
Spore-forming gram-positive anaerobe; spores survive alcohol hand rubs, so wash with soap and water.
Toxin A (enterotoxin) draws fluid and neutrophils; toxin B (cytotoxin) breaks down the actin cytoskeleton.
Yellow-white pseudomembranes of fibrin, mucus, and neutrophils; watery diarrhea, cramps, high white count.
Diagnosis: stool toxin or toxin gene (PCR) testing. Severe cases cause toxic megacolon.
Bloody (invasive or cytotoxic): Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella, EHEC, Entamoeba histolytica.
EHEC O157:H7 (undercooked beef): Shiga toxin damages renal endothelium, causing hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Campylobacter (poultry) can trigger Guillain-Barre syndrome by molecular mimicry.
Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella, and Yersinia can trigger HLA-B27 reactive arthritis.
Watery: rotavirus (unvaccinated infants), norovirus (cruise ships, institutions), ETEC (traveler's diarrhea).
Cholera toxin keeps Gs on, cAMP rises, and CFTR pumps chloride and water out: rice-water stool.
Bacillus cereus emetic toxin is preformed in reheated rice and causes vomiting within hours.
Plaque biofilm at the gum line causes gingivitis: red, swollen gums that bleed; reversible.
Periodontitis: Porphyromonas gingivalis and host inflammation destroy periodontal ligament and alveolar bone.
Streptococcus mutans ferments sugar to acid, dissolving enamel (caries) and leading to tooth abscess.
Oral thrush: Candida albicans; white plaques that scrape off; infants, inhaled steroids, antibiotics, diabetes, HIV.
Herpetic gingivostomatitis (primary HSV-1): fever with vesicles on gums and lips. Herpangina (coxsackie A): vesicles on the soft palate and posterior pharynx.
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease: coxsackie A16, mouth ulcers plus palm and sole vesicles. Aphthous ulcers: Crohn disease, Behcet disease.
Infectious esophagitis in immunosuppression: Candida (white plaques), HSV-1 (punched-out ulcers), CMV (linear ulcers).
HBV chronic: most infected neonates, few infected adults. HCV chronic: most infected adults.
HBV and HCV lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; HBV can cause carcinoma without cirrhosis.
HCV causes mixed cryoglobulinemia (vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, purpura).
Pyogenic liver abscess: biliary or portal spread, often E. coli or Klebsiella.
Amebic liver abscess: Entamoeba histolytica, travel history, anchovy paste fluid.

tricks.label: Read HBV serology in order
tricks.text: First ask about HBsAg (virus present now). Then anti-HBc (ever infected; IgM recent, IgG old). Then anti-HBs (immune). Anti-HBs alone means vaccine; IgM anti-HBc alone means window period.

tricks.label: Scrape test
tricks.text: White plaque that wipes off is thrush. White plaque that stays is leukoplakia or hairy leukoplakia.

tricks.label: Which way the chronic odds run
tricks.text: HBV becomes chronic in most newborns and few adults because the newborn immune system tolerates the virus. HCV becomes chronic in most adults because its envelope proteins keep changing and escape antibodies.

highYield: Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and cephalosporins predispose to C. difficile colitis; diagnose by stool toxin or toxin gene testing.
EHEC O157:H7 leads to hemolytic uremic syndrome; Campylobacter leads to Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Rice-water stool from contaminated water means Vibrio cholerae.
IgM anti-HBc alone means the hepatitis B window period; anti-HBs alone means vaccination.
HCV becomes chronic in most adults and causes mixed cryoglobulinemia.
CMV esophagitis has linear ulcers and inclusions in endothelial and stromal cells; HSV has punched-out ulcers with intranuclear inclusions in squamous cells.
Herpangina (coxsackie A) affects the posterior mouth; primary HSV-1 gingivostomatitis affects the gums and lips.
Amebic liver abscess fluid looks like anchovy paste.
pitfalls: Alcohol hand gel does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water does.
Anti-HBs alone means vaccine immunity; anti-HBs with IgG anti-HBc means past infection that cleared.
Gingivitis is reversible; periodontitis means bone and ligament are already lost.
Aphthous ulcers are not preceded by vesicles; vesicles that break into ulcers point to HSV or coxsackie virus.
A single gram-negative rod in a liver abscess with biliary disease suggests pyogenic abscess; a young traveler with a single right-lobe abscess suggests amebic abscess.
